The big picture

A sequence converges to a limit a if, for every tolerance \varepsilon > 0, all terms from some index N on lie in the \varepsilon-neighbourhood (a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon); a sequence that converges to no real number is divergent, and it may or may not tend to \pm\infty. Sequences with limit 0 are infinitesimal. With the definition in hand, the lecture builds a toolkit so that most limits never need \varepsilon again: the limit is unique, limits respect +, -, \cdot, / (unless an indeterminate form such as \infty - \infty appears), they preserve \le, the squeeze theorem traps a sequence between two others, and a catalogue of standard limits (p^n, \sqrt[n]{c}, c^n/n!) covers the usual building blocks. The monotone convergence theorem proves convergence without knowing the limit: bounded and monotone is enough. That gives Euler's number e, and a different route uses subsequences: by the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence, the possible subsequential limits are exactly the accumulation points from 6 Sequences, and the smallest and largest of them are the limit inferior and limit superior. Finally, a Cauchy sequence (late terms close to each other) is the same as a convergent one in \mathbb{R}, which again certifies convergence without naming the limit.

Why limits?

The first few terms suggest a pattern. A limit lets us say precisely whether the terms approach a fixed number.

Recall our approximation of \sqrt2:

a_1 = 1, \qquad a_{n+1} = \frac12\left(a_n + \frac{2}{a_n}\right): \qquad 1,\ 1.5,\ 1.4167,\ 1.4142,\ \dots
Symbols
  • a_n — the n-th approximation of \sqrt2 (a_n > 0); a_1 = 1 is the starting guess
  • a_{n+1} — the next approximation: the average of a_n and \frac{2}{a_n}

Do the terms really approach \sqrt2? (Answered on slide 58: Newton's iteration for √2.)

When is the robot close enough?

An idealised robot moves half the remaining distance towards its docking point at 2 m with every command. It starts at x_1 = 0.

Successive positions:

x_{n+1} = x_n + \frac{2 - x_n}{2}: \qquad 0,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 1.75,\ 1.875,\ \dots
Symbols
  • x_n — the robot's position after n - 1 commands (m), measured along the track from the start; x_1 = 0
  • 2 — the docking point (m); 2 - x_n — the remaining distance, of which half is covered per command

The positions get closer to the docking point. Questions: Does x_n ever equal 2? When is the error less than 1 cm?

Answer: x_n = 2 - 2^{2-n} < 2 for every n, but x_n \to 2. By n = 9 (eight corrections), the remaining error is 1/128 m \approx 0.78 cm.

Why is x_n = 2 - 2^{2-n}, and why n = 9?

Write the error as e_n = 2 - x_n. The recursion gives e_{n+1} = 2 - x_n - \frac{2 - x_n}{2} = \frac{e_n}{2}: the error halves with every command, a geometric sequence (6 Sequences › Arithmetic and geometric sequences) with e_1 = 2 and ratio \frac12. So e_n = 2 \cdot \left(\frac12\right)^{n-1} = 2^{2-n}, which is never 0, so the robot never arrives. Error below 1 cm = 0.01 m means 2^{n-2} > 100; since 2^6 = 64 and 2^7 = 128, this first holds for n - 2 = 7, i.e. n = 9, with error 2^{-7} = \frac{1}{128} m.

Intuition

"Never equal to 2, yet the limit is 2" is the whole point of the chapter: a limit is not a term the sequence reaches but a value that the terms get and stay arbitrarily close to. The engineering question "when is the error below 1 cm?" is exactly the \varepsilon–N question of the definition below, with \varepsilon = 0.01 m and answer N = 9.

A few typical behaviours

Approaches zeroKeeps oscillatingGrows without bound
a_n = 1/nb_n = (-1)^nc_n = n
a_n \to 0no finite limitc_n \to +\infty

Three small plots on the slide: falling points that level off near 0; points jumping between two heights; points rising along a straight line.

These are some common ways a sequence can behave.

Oscillating sequences can also converge

Both sequences change sign, but the size of their terms behaves differently.

  • Oscillation without convergence: a_n = (-1)^n. The terms stay a fixed distance 1 from zero.
  • Oscillation towards zero: b_n = \frac{(-1)^n}{n}. The distance to zero is \lvert b_n\rvert = 1/n \to 0.
Common mistake — "an oscillating sequence cannot converge"

Tempting: a sequence that keeps changing sign never "settles", so it has no limit. But convergence only asks that the distance \lvert a_n - a\rvert shrinks to 0, not that the terms approach from one side. \frac{(-1)^n}{n} jumps from side to side forever, and still every term after n = 100 is within 0.01 of 0. What kills convergence for (-1)^n is not the sign change but the fact that the jumps keep size 2.

Definition of convergence

A real sequence (a_n) converges to a \in \mathbb{R} if

\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists N \in \mathbb{N}\ \ \forall n \ge N : \quad \lvert a_n - a\rvert < \varepsilon.

If such a real number a exists, then a is called a limit of the sequence, and (a_n) is called convergent. We write

\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = a \qquad \text{or} \qquad a_n \to a.
Symbols
  • a_n — the n-th term; a \in \mathbb{R} — the candidate limit
  • \varepsilon — a tolerance: any positive number, however small
  • N — an index "from which on" the tolerance is met; it may depend on \varepsilon
  • \lvert a_n - a\rvert — the distance between the term and the limit (3 Set of Real Numbers › Absolute value as distance)
  • \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n, a_n \to a — read "the limit of a_n as n tends to infinity", "a_n tends to a"

In plain language: No matter how narrow a band we draw around a, we can go far enough along the sequence that every term from then on lies inside it. The index N may depend on how small we choose \varepsilon.

Intuition — a challenge and a response

Read the quantifiers as a game. A sceptic names a tolerance \varepsilon ("I want every term within 0.001 of a"). You must answer with an index N ("from term N on, that holds"). The sequence converges to a if you can answer every challenge, however small. The order matters: \varepsilon comes first and N is allowed to depend on it, since a stricter tolerance usually needs a later start. A proof that a_n \to a is therefore a recipe for N in terms of \varepsilon.

Connection

Compare the accumulation point definition from 6 Sequences › Accumulation points of a sequence: "\forall \varepsilon\ \forall N\ \exists n \ge N" (infinitely many terms come close). Convergence demands "\forall \varepsilon\ \exists N\ \forall n \ge N" (all late terms are close). Only two quantifiers swap, but the second statement is much stronger: a limit is always an accumulation point, while (-1)^n has two accumulation points and no limit.

What does "eventually close" mean?

For the plotted sequence a_n = 1 + \frac{7(-1)^{n+1}}{8n}, we investigate the limit a = 1 with tolerance \varepsilon_1 = 0.20.

The band extends across all indices. Since \lvert a_n - 1\rvert = \frac{7}{8n} < 0.20 for n \ge 5, all terms from N_1 = 5 onward stay inside it.

A smaller neighbourhood. Now ask for greater accuracy: \varepsilon_2 = 0.10 < \varepsilon_1 = 0.20. Can the same sequence eventually stay in this narrower band? Now \lvert a_n - 1\rvert = \frac{7}{8n} < 0.10 for all n \ge 9. The smaller tolerance requires a later index in this example.

Where do N_1 = 5 and N_2 = 9 come from?

\lvert a_n - 1\rvert = \left\lvert \frac{7(-1)^{n+1}}{8n}\right\rvert = \frac{7}{8n}, because \lvert(-1)^{n+1}\rvert = 1. Then \frac{7}{8n} < 0.2 \iff n > \frac{7}{1.6} = 4.375, so the first integer is 5. And \frac{7}{8n} < 0.1 \iff n > 8.75, so the first integer is 9. Since \frac{7}{8n} decreases in n, once a term is inside the band all later ones are too, which is what "\forall n \ge N" asks.

Convergence and neighbourhoods

For a \in \mathbb{R} and \varepsilon > 0, the \varepsilon-neighbourhood of a is

U(a, \varepsilon) = (a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon).

The two conditions say the same thing ("less than \varepsilon away from a"):

\lvert a_n - a\rvert < \varepsilon \iff a_n \in U(a, \varepsilon).

Equivalent definition of convergence:

a_n \to a \iff \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists N \in \mathbb{N}\ \ \forall n \ge N : \ a_n \in U(a, \varepsilon).
Symbols
  • U(a, \varepsilon) — the open interval of radius \varepsilon around a (centre a, half-width \varepsilon)
  • a, \varepsilon, N, n — as in the definition above
Connection

These are the neighbourhoods of 3 Set of Real Numbers › Neighbourhoods. In this language: every neighbourhood of a contains all but finitely many terms. "All but finitely many" is the same as "from some N on", since a finite set of indices has a largest element.

Proving limits from the definition

Proof: \frac1n \to 0

Given any \varepsilon > 0, find an index N such that \lvert 1/n - 0\rvert < \varepsilon whenever n \ge N.

\frac1n < \varepsilon \iff n > \frac1\varepsilon.

Choose N = \left\lfloor \frac1\varepsilon \right\rfloor + 1. Then, for every n \ge N,

\left\lvert \frac1n - 0\right\rvert = \frac1n \le \frac1N < \varepsilon.

Thus \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac1n = 0.

Symbols
  • \lfloor x \rfloor — the floor of x: the greatest integer \le x (5 Functions › Floor and ceiling: small changes, big jumps)
  • N = \lfloor 1/\varepsilon \rfloor + 1 — the first integer strictly larger than \frac1\varepsilon
  • \frac1n \le \frac1N — holds because n \ge N and both are positive
Why exactly N = \lfloor 1/\varepsilon \rfloor + 1?

The scratch work says we need N > \frac1\varepsilon, and N must be a natural number. \lfloor \frac1\varepsilon \rfloor \le \frac1\varepsilon might be too small (it can equal \frac1\varepsilon), but adding 1 gives a number strictly larger, so \frac1N < \varepsilon. Any larger N would work too; the definition only asks for some N, not the smallest. That an integer above \frac1\varepsilon exists at all is the Archimedean property (3 Set of Real Numbers › Archimedean property).

Another proof: n/(n+1) → 1

a_n = \frac{n}{n+1} = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1}, \qquad \lvert a_n - 1\rvert = \frac{1}{n+1}.
Symbols
  • a_n = \frac{n}{n+1} — the sequence from the worked example in 6 Sequences › Monotonicity of a sequence; \frac{1}{n+1} — its distance to the proposed limit 1

If n > 1/\varepsilon, then 1/(n+1) < \varepsilon. Therefore \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{n+1} = 1.

Plot on the slide: every term is below 1, but the distance becomes arbitrarily small.

Worked example — an \varepsilon–N proof that \frac{3n+1}{n+2} \to 3
  1. Compute the distance to the candidate limit and simplify: \frac{3n+1}{n+2} - 3 = \frac{3n + 1 - 3n - 6}{n+2} = \frac{-5}{n+2}, so \lvert a_n - 3\rvert = \frac{5}{n+2}.
  2. Scratch work — solve "distance < \varepsilon" for n: \frac{5}{n+2} < \varepsilon \iff n > \frac5\varepsilon - 2.
  3. Choose N (any integer above the threshold will do): N = \left\lfloor \frac5\varepsilon \right\rfloor + 1 > \frac5\varepsilon - 2.
  4. Write the proof forwards: for n \ge N, \lvert a_n - 3\rvert = \frac{5}{n+2} \le \frac{5}{N+2} < \varepsilon.
  5. Sanity check with a number: \varepsilon = 0.1 gives N = 51 and \lvert a_{51} - 3\rvert = \frac{5}{53} \approx 0.094 < 0.1. (The smallest N that works is 49; the proof doesn't need it.)

A limit with square roots

Evaluate \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(\sqrt{n+1} - \sqrt n\right). Multiply by the conjugate:

\sqrt{n+1} - \sqrt n = \frac{(n+1) - n}{\sqrt{n+1} + \sqrt n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1} + \sqrt n}.
Symbols
  • \sqrt{n+1} + \sqrt n — the conjugate of \sqrt{n+1} - \sqrt n; multiplying and dividing by it uses (x - y)(x + y) = x^2 - y^2

Because

0 < \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1} + \sqrt n} \le \frac{1}{2\sqrt n} \to 0, \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(\sqrt{n+1} - \sqrt n\right) = 0.
Symbols
  • \frac{1}{2\sqrt n} — an upper bound obtained by making the denominator smaller: \sqrt{n+1} \ge \sqrt n
Intuition

Both \sqrt{n+1} and \sqrt n grow without bound, so the difference is of the form \infty - \infty, which by itself says nothing (see Indeterminate forms are warnings). The conjugate turns the difference into a quotient whose behaviour is visible. The last step is the squeeze idea from later in the lecture: the sequence sits between 0 and something that tends to 0.

Divergence

How to show that a sequence diverges

Lemma. A real sequence (a_n) is divergent if and only if

\forall a \in \mathbb{R}\ \ \exists \varepsilon > 0\ \ \forall N \in \mathbb{N}\ \ \exists n \ge N : \quad \lvert a_n - a\rvert \ge \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • a — any real number tried as a limit
  • \varepsilon — a distance that terms keep reaching; it may depend on a
  • N, n — however far along we go (N), there is a later term a_n at distance \ge \varepsilon from a

In words: Whatever real number a we try as a limit, there is a distance \varepsilon > 0 such that terms at least that far from a keep appearing, no matter how far along the sequence we go. Why? This is the negation of the convergence condition: not all sufficiently late terms stay close to a. We mean infinitely many indices, not necessarily infinitely many distinct values.

Intuition — "divergent"

A sequence is divergent if it is not convergent, i.e. there is no real number a with a_n \to a. This covers very different behaviours: oscillating ((-1)^n), running off to +\infty (n), or both (n(-1)^n). Tending to \pm\infty is one kind of divergence, not the opposite of it.

Why is the lemma exactly the negation of convergence?

"Divergent" = "for no a \in \mathbb{R} does a_n \to a" = \forall a \in \mathbb{R}:\ \neg(a_n \to a). Negate \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists N\ \forall n \ge N : \lvert a_n - a\rvert < \varepsilon using the rules of 1 Elements of Logic › Negating quantified statements: every \forall becomes \exists, every \exists becomes \forall, and the inner statement is negated, < becoming \ge. That gives \exists \varepsilon > 0\ \forall N\ \exists n \ge N : \lvert a_n - a\rvert \ge \varepsilon. The restrictions "> 0" and "n \ge N" stay where they are; they describe the range of the variable, not the claim.

Why (-1)^n does not converge

a_n = (-1)^n keeps taking both values -1 and 1, however large n becomes.

Suppose a_n \to a for some a \in \mathbb{R}. Choose \varepsilon = \frac12. Eventually, both -1 and 1 would have to be within distance \frac12 of a. But the triangle inequality gives

2 = \lvert 1 - (-1)\rvert \le \lvert 1 - a\rvert + \lvert a + 1\rvert < 1,

which is impossible. Thus (a_n) diverges.

Symbols
  • a — the supposed limit; \varepsilon = \frac12 — the tolerance chosen to reach a contradiction
  • \lvert 1 - a\rvert < \frac12 — from a late even-indexed term (a_n = 1); \lvert a + 1\rvert = \lvert a - (-1)\rvert < \frac12 — from a late odd-indexed term
  • the middle step is the triangle inequality (3 Set of Real Numbers › Absolute value: useful properties) applied to 1 - (-1) = (1 - a) + (a + 1)

Practice: Khan Academy – convergence and divergence of sequences (linked on slides 14, 20 and 32).

Intuition

The choice \varepsilon = \frac12 is not magic: any \varepsilon \le 1 works. The two values are 2 apart, and a window of total width 2\varepsilon \le 2 cannot hold both -1 and 1 (strictly inside). Since both values occur at arbitrarily late indices, no window around any a can contain all late terms.

Infinite limits

For a real sequence (a_n), the following statements mean that terms eventually exceed any prescribed size.

Tends (diverges) to +\infty:

\forall M > 0\ \ \exists N\ \ \forall n \ge N : \ a_n > M.

Tends (diverges) to -\infty:

\forall M > 0\ \ \exists N\ \ \forall n \ge N : \ a_n < -M.

Infinitely large sequence:

\forall M > 0\ \ \exists N\ \ \forall n \ge N : \ \lvert a_n\rvert > M.
Symbols
  • M — a size threshold, however large (plays the role of \varepsilon)
  • N — the index from which on all terms beat the threshold; it may depend on M
  • written a_n \to +\infty, a_n \to -\infty, \lvert a_n\rvert \to \infty

Example: a_n = n(-1)^n satisfies neither a_n \to +\infty nor a_n \to -\infty, but \lvert a_n\rvert \to \infty.

An infinite limit is not a finite real limit. Not every divergent sequence tends to infinity.

Connection

Compare 6 Sequences › Infinite accumulation points: "+\infty is an extended accumulation point" means infinitely many terms exceed every M; "a_n \to +\infty" means all late terms do. n(-1)^n has both +\infty and -\infty as extended accumulation points, but tends to neither.

Infinitesimal sequences

A real sequence (a_n) is called infinitesimal if \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0.

Examples: \frac1n \to 0, \frac{(-1)^n}{n} \to 0. Another example: \frac1n \sin\frac{\pi n}{2} \to 0.

Useful facts:

  • sums and scalar multiples of infinitesimals are infinitesimal;
  • an infinitesimal times a bounded sequence is infinitesimal;
  • a_n \to a iff a_n = a + \alpha_n with \alpha_n \to 0.
Why do these three facts hold?
  • Third fact: put \alpha_n := a_n - a. Then \lvert \alpha_n - 0\rvert = \lvert a_n - a\rvert, so the two definitions "\alpha_n \to 0" and "a_n \to a" are word for word the same condition.
  • Bounded times infinitesimal: if \lvert b_n\rvert \le C (with C > 0) and \alpha_n \to 0, then \lvert \alpha_n b_n\rvert \le C\lvert \alpha_n\rvert. Given \varepsilon, choose N with \lvert\alpha_n\rvert < \frac{\varepsilon}{C} for n \ge N; then \lvert \alpha_n b_n\rvert < \varepsilon.
  • Example: \sin\frac{\pi n}{2} runs through 1, 0, -1, 0, \dots (bounded by 1) and \frac1n \to 0, so the product tends to 0, although \sin\frac{\pi n}{2} itself has no limit.
  • Sums: the \frac\varepsilon2 argument in Arithmetic of finite limits.

A limit is unique

Theorem. A real sequence cannot converge to two different real numbers.

Proof by contradiction. Suppose a_n \to a and a_n \to b with a \neq b. Take \varepsilon = \lvert a - b\rvert/3. For all sufficiently large n,

\lvert a_n - a\rvert < \varepsilon, \qquad \lvert a_n - b\rvert < \varepsilon.

The triangle inequality gives

\lvert a - b\rvert \le \lvert a - a_n\rvert + \lvert a_n - b\rvert < 2\varepsilon = \tfrac23 \lvert a - b\rvert,

a contradiction. \square

Symbols
  • a, b — the two supposed limits; \lvert a - b\rvert > 0 — the distance between them
  • \varepsilon = \frac{\lvert a - b\rvert}{3} — a tolerance small enough that the two \varepsilon-neighbourhoods do not overlap
  • "sufficiently large n" — n \ge \max\{N_a, N_b\}, where N_a, N_b are the indices from the two convergence statements
  • \square — end of proof
Why \varepsilon = |a - b|/3, and why may we use one n for both?

We need two windows around a and b that cannot both contain a_n. Any \varepsilon \le \frac{\lvert a - b\rvert}{2} does it; \frac13 just makes the final inequality strict with room to spare (\frac23\lvert a - b\rvert < \lvert a - b\rvert needs \lvert a - b\rvert > 0, true since a \neq b). Each convergence gives its own index, N_a and N_b; every n \ge \max\{N_a, N_b\} satisfies both inequalities at once. Taking the maximum of finitely many indices is the standard move in every proof that combines two limits. (Proof by contradiction: 1 Elements of Logic › Proof by contradiction.)

This is why we may write "the limit" and \lim a_n = a with an equals sign.

Arithmetic of limits

Arithmetic of finite limits

Suppose a_n \to a \in \mathbb{R} and b_n \to b \in \mathbb{R}. Then:

\lim_{n \to \infty} (c a_n + d b_n) = c a + d b, \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} (a_n b_n) = a b,
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \frac{a}{b} \quad (b \neq 0), \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} \lvert a_n\rvert = \lvert a\rvert.
Symbols
  • a, b — the (finite) limits of (a_n) and (b_n)
  • c, d — fixed real numbers (constants, not depending on n)
  • \frac{a_n}{b_n} — the termwise quotient (6 Sequences › Operations with sequences)

For the quotient, b_n \neq 0 is needed for all sufficiently large n; b \neq 0 guarantees this. Powers and roots also require their expressions to be defined.

Why does the limit of a sum equal the sum of the limits (and why the product)?

Sum (c = d = 1): given \varepsilon > 0, use each convergence with tolerance \frac\varepsilon2: from some N on, \lvert a_n - a\rvert < \frac\varepsilon2 and \lvert b_n - b\rvert < \frac\varepsilon2. Then by the triangle inequality \lvert (a_n + b_n) - (a + b)\rvert \le \lvert a_n - a\rvert + \lvert b_n - b\rvert < \varepsilon. Product: write a_n b_n - ab = (a_n - a) b_n + a(b_n - b). The first part is infinitesimal times bounded ((b_n) converges, so it is bounded, see Convergence and boundedness), the second is a constant times an infinitesimal. Both tend to 0, so a_n b_n \to ab by the facts in Infinitesimal sequences. Why "b_n \neq 0 eventually": with \varepsilon = \frac{\lvert b\rvert}{2}, late terms satisfy \lvert b_n\rvert > \frac{\lvert b\rvert}{2} > 0.

Common mistake — using the rules backwards

The rules say: if both limits exist, then the sum/product has the expected limit. They don't say that a convergent sum comes from convergent pieces. a_n = (-1)^n and b_n = (-1)^{n+1} both diverge, yet a_n + b_n = 0 converges. So "\lim(a_n + b_n) = \lim a_n + \lim b_n" may only be written after checking that the right-hand limits exist and are finite (or form no indeterminate form, below).

Arithmetic with infinite limits

Some rules extend to infinite limits, provided no indeterminate form occurs.

With finite a \in \mathbb{R}:

a + (\pm\infty) = \pm\infty, \qquad \frac{a}{\pm\infty} = 0, \qquad a \cdot (\pm\infty) = \begin{cases} \pm\infty, & a > 0, \\ \mp\infty, & a < 0. \end{cases}

With infinite limits:

+\infty + \infty = +\infty, \quad -\infty - \infty = -\infty, \quad (\pm\infty) \cdot (\pm\infty) = +\infty, \quad (\pm\infty) \cdot (\mp\infty) = -\infty.
Symbols
  • each rule is shorthand for a statement about sequences: e.g. "a + (+\infty) = +\infty" means: if a_n \to a \in \mathbb{R} and b_n \to +\infty, then a_n + b_n \to +\infty
  • \pm, \mp — read top signs together and bottom signs together: a \cdot (+\infty) = +\infty for a > 0 and a \cdot (+\infty) = -\infty for a < 0

Important: The following are indeterminate forms:

\infty - \infty, \qquad 0 \cdot \infty, \qquad \frac\infty\infty, \qquad \infty^0.

Their limits require further analysis.

Symbols
  • each form names a type of expression, not a number: e.g. "\infty - \infty" is a_n - b_n with a_n \to +\infty and b_n \to +\infty
Intuition — what "indeterminate" means

An indeterminate form is a combination where knowing the limits of the pieces does not determine the limit of the whole: different sequences with the same type give different results (next section). It doesn't mean "the limit doesn't exist"; it means "you have to rewrite the expression and look again".

Calculating a rational limit

Find

\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n^2 + 4n - 5}{2n^2 + 3n - 100}.

Divide numerator and denominator by n^2:

\frac{n^2 + 4n - 5}{2n^2 + 3n - 100} = \frac{1 + 4/n - 5/n^2}{2 + 3/n - 100/n^2}, \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1 + 4/n - 5/n^2}{2 + 3/n - 100/n^2} = \frac12.
Symbols
  • n^2 — the highest power of n in the denominator; dividing by it turns every other term into an infinitesimal (\frac4n, \frac{5}{n^2}, … \to 0)
  • the result \frac12 — the ratio of the leading coefficients 1 and 2
Why is dividing by n^2 allowed and why does it help?

Dividing numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number doesn't change the fraction, so each term of the sequence is unchanged. Before, the quotient is of type \frac\infty\infty (indeterminate). After, numerator \to 1 + 0 - 0 = 1 and denominator \to 2 + 0 - 0 = 2 \neq 0, using \frac1n \to 0, \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac1n \cdot \frac1n \to 0 and the sum/product/quotient rules, which now apply because every piece has a finite limit.

Comparing polynomial degrees

Larger degree in the denominatorLarger degree in the numeratorEqual degrees
\dfrac{3n + 1}{n^2 + 2} \to 0\dfrac{5n^6 - 1}{10n^4 - n^2} \to +\infty\dfrac{n^2 + 4n}{2n^2 + 1} \to \dfrac12

Compare leading powers, but also check the eventual sign of the denominator.

Worked example — two rational limits, one with a sign trap

(a) \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \frac{3n^2 - n}{5 - 2n^2}.

  1. Compare degrees: both are degree 2, so the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients.
  2. Divide by n^2: \frac{3 - 1/n}{5/n^2 - 2} \to \frac{3}{-2} = -\frac32. The leading coefficient of the denominator is -2, not 2.

(b) \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \frac{n^3 + 1}{1 - n^2}.

  1. Compare degrees: 3 above, 2 below, so the quotient is unbounded.
  2. Find the sign: the numerator is positive; the denominator 1 - n^2 < 0 for every n \ge 2. So the terms are eventually negative: a_2 = -3, a_3 = -3.5, a_4 \approx -4.33.
  3. Conclude: \frac{n^3 + 1}{1 - n^2} = \frac{n + 1/n^2}{1/n^2 - 1}; the numerator \to +\infty and the denominator \to -1, so the limit is -\infty, not +\infty.

Indeterminate forms are warnings

Finite-limit algebra does not allow us to treat \infty as an ordinary number.

Both terms tend to +\infty:But with another pair:
a_n = n + 1, b_n = na_n = 2n, b_n = n
a_n - b_n = 1a_n - b_n = n \to +\infty

The form \infty - \infty does not determine a limit. Similarly, 0 \cdot \infty, 0/0 and \infty/\infty require further work.

Common mistake — "\infty - \infty = 0", "\frac\infty\infty = 1", "1^\infty = 1"

Tempting: treat \infty like a big number that cancels itself. The table above already shows \infty - \infty giving 1 or +\infty. Likewise \frac{2n}{n} \to 2 and \frac{n^2}{n} \to +\infty are both \frac\infty\infty. The trap that survives longest is 1^\infty: 1 + \frac1n \to 1, and "1 to any power is 1", so \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n \to 1? No — it tends to e \approx 2.718 (slide 37), and \left(1 + \frac2n\right)^n \to e^2 \approx 7.39. The base approaches 1 while the exponent grows, and the two effects compete. Each such limit needs its own rewriting.

Limits and inequalities

Passing inequalities to the limit

Lemma. If a_n \le b_n for all sufficiently large n, and a_n \to a, b_n \to b, then a \le b.

Strict inequalities need care: a_n = 0, b_n = \frac1n: a_n < b_n for all n, but \lim a_n = \lim b_n = 0.

A useful converse direction: If a_n \to a and b_n \to b with a < b, then a_n < b_n for all sufficiently large n.

Why does a_n \le b_n give a \le b?

Suppose instead a > b. Apply the "converse direction" with the roles swapped: b < a gives b_n < a_n for all large n, contradicting a_n \le b_n. And the converse direction itself: take \varepsilon = \frac{b - a}{2}; for large n, a_n < a + \varepsilon = \frac{a + b}{2} = b - \varepsilon < b_n. In words: once both sequences are inside non-overlapping windows around a and b, their order is the order of the windows.

The squeeze (sandwich) theorem

Theorem. Let (a_n), (b_n) and (c_n) be real sequences. If there exists N \in \mathbb{N} such that a_n \le b_n \le c_n for all n \ge N, and \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} c_n = L \in \mathbb{R}, then

\lim_{n \to \infty} b_n = L.
Symbols
  • (a_n), (c_n) — the lower and upper "bread", both converging to the same L
  • (b_n) — the sequence trapped between them from index N on; its limit is what we want
  • L — the common limit, a real number

Example:

-\frac1n \le \frac{\cos n}{n} \le \frac1n.

Since both outer sequences tend to 0,

\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\cos n}{n} = 0.
Symbols
  • \cos n — the cosine of n radians; only its bound -1 \le \cos n \le 1 is used, divided by n > 0

Proof. Suppose a_n \le b_n \le c_n for n \ge n_0, with a_n, c_n \to L. Given \varepsilon > 0, choose N so that for n \ge N,

L - \varepsilon < a_n \quad\text{and}\quad c_n < L + \varepsilon.

For n \ge \max\{N, n_0\},

L - \varepsilon < a_n \le b_n \le c_n < L + \varepsilon.

Thus \lvert b_n - L\rvert < \varepsilon, proving b_n \to L. \square

Symbols
  • n_0 — the index from which the sandwich a_n \le b_n \le c_n holds (the theorem's N)
  • N — the index from which both a_n and c_n are within \varepsilon of L (one index for both, by taking a maximum as in A limit is unique)
Intuition

The squeeze theorem is the main tool when the sequence contains something that has no limit but is bounded (\cos n, \sin n, (-1)^n): bound that factor, and squeeze. Note that we never need to know anything about b_n except that it is trapped; the limit of b_n is not assumed to exist, the theorem proves it.

Worked example — \lim \sqrt[n]{2^n + 3^n} by squeezing
  1. Find the dominant term: 3^n is larger than 2^n, so 3^n \le 2^n + 3^n \le 3^n + 3^n = 2 \cdot 3^n.
  2. Take n-th roots (the root is increasing, so the order is kept): 3 \le \sqrt[n]{2^n + 3^n} \le \sqrt[n]{2} \cdot 3.
  3. Limits of the bread: the left side is constantly 3; the right side tends to 1 \cdot 3 = 3 by \sqrt[n]{c} \to 1 (Common limits: n-th root) and the product rule.
  4. Squeeze: \sqrt[n]{2^n + 3^n} \to 3. Check: n = 5 gives \approx 3.075, n = 20 gives \approx 3.00005.

Changing a finite number of terms

Changing, removing, or inserting finitely many initial terms does not change a sequence's limit (if it exists).

a_n = \frac1n \to 0; \qquad b_1 = 100, \quad b_2 = -50, \quad b_n = \frac1n \ (n \ge 3).
Symbols
  • (b_n) — the sequence \frac1n with its first two terms replaced by 100 and -50

The sequence (b_n) still converges to 0. The definition only refers to what happens after some index N. The squeeze theorem also works when the inequalities hold only for all sufficiently large indices.

Corollaries: comparing limits

Let (a_n) and (b_n) be real sequences such that

\exists N \in \mathbb{N}\ \ \forall n \ge N : \quad a_n \le b_n.

Finite limits:

a_n \to a \in \mathbb{R}, \quad b_n \to b \in \mathbb{R} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad a \le b.

Infinite limits:

a_n \to +\infty \ \Longrightarrow\ b_n \to +\infty, \qquad b_n \to -\infty \ \Longrightarrow\ a_n \to -\infty.
Symbols
  • a_n \le b_n — (a_n) is the smaller sequence (from index N on)
  • a, b — the finite limits; \pm\infty — infinite limits in the sense of Infinite limits

The inequalities need to hold only from some index onward.

Intuition

The infinite version is a "one-sided squeeze": a sequence pushed up by something going to +\infty must go to +\infty too; no upper bread is needed. Example: n + \sin n \ge n - 1 \to +\infty, so n + \sin n \to +\infty.

Common limits

Powers

For p \in \mathbb{R},

\lim_{n \to \infty} p^n = \begin{cases} 0, & \lvert p\rvert < 1, \\ 1, & p = 1, \\ +\infty, & p > 1. \end{cases}
Symbols
  • p — a fixed real base; p^n — the geometric sequence with first term p and ratio p

Examples: \left(\frac12\right)^n \to 0, 2^n \to +\infty.

For p = -1, the sequence oscillates. If p < -1, its magnitude grows but the sign alternates.

Why powers behave differently

The cases p > 1 and \lvert p\rvert < 1 follow from two simple inequalities.

If p = 1 + h > 1:

p^n = (1 + h)^n \ge 1 + nh \longrightarrow +\infty

by Bernoulli's inequality.

If 0 < \lvert p\rvert < 1:

q = \frac{1}{\lvert p\rvert} > 1, \qquad \lvert p\rvert^n = \frac{1}{q^n} \to 0.

Since -\lvert p\rvert^n \le p^n \le \lvert p\rvert^n, the squeeze theorem gives p^n \to 0.

Symbols
  • h = p - 1 > 0 — how much the base exceeds 1
  • q = \frac{1}{\lvert p\rvert} — the reciprocal of the base's size, larger than 1 so q^n \to +\infty by the first case
  • Bernoulli's inequality: (1 + t)^n \ge 1 + nt for t \ge -1, n \in \mathbb{N} (5 Functions › Optional reference: inequalities)
Intuition

Bernoulli replaces the exponential (1 + h)^n by the much smaller straight line 1 + nh, and even the straight line goes to +\infty (Archimedes). The case \lvert p\rvert < 1 is then the reciprocal of the case p > 1, and negative bases are handled by squeezing between \pm\lvert p\rvert^n. The case p = 0 is trivial (all terms 0).

Common limits: n-th root

For any constant c > 0,

\lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{c} = 1.
Symbols
  • c — a fixed positive number; \sqrt[n]{c} = c^{1/n} — its n-th root

Idea of proof for c > 1: Let u_n = c^{1/n} - 1 > 0. Bernoulli's inequality gives

c = (1 + u_n)^n \ge 1 + n u_n \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0 < u_n \le \frac{c - 1}{n} \to 0.
Symbols
  • u_n — the amount by which \sqrt[n]{c} exceeds 1; showing u_n \to 0 (by squeezing) shows \sqrt[n]{c} \to 1
  • c = (1 + u_n)^n — because 1 + u_n = c^{1/n}

For 0 < c < 1, apply the result to 1/c and take reciprocals.

Factorials versus exponentials

For every fixed c \in \mathbb{R},

\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{c^n}{n!} = 0.

Why? If c = 0, every term is zero. Otherwise, the ratio of successive magnitudes is

\frac{\lvert c\rvert^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{\lvert c\rvert^n/n!} = \frac{\lvert c\rvert}{n + 1}.

For large n this is at most 1/2, so the terms decrease at least geometrically.

Symbols
  • n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdots n — n factorial
  • \frac{\lvert c\rvert}{n+1} — the factor by which the size of a term changes from index n to n + 1

Related result: \sqrt[n]{n!} \to +\infty. Factorial growth eventually dominates any fixed exponential base.

Why does "ratio at most \frac12" force the limit 0?

Let x_n = \frac{\lvert c\rvert^n}{n!}. The ratio \frac{\lvert c\rvert}{n+1} \le \frac12 as soon as n + 1 \ge 2\lvert c\rvert; call the first such index n_0. From there each step at least halves: x_{n_0 + k} \le x_{n_0} \left(\frac12\right)^k. The right side tends to 0 (Powers), so 0 \le x_n \le (something \to 0), and by squeezing x_n \to 0. Then -x_n \le \frac{c^n}{n!} \le x_n handles negative c. Example c = 5: the ratio \frac{5}{n+1} is \le \frac12 from n = 9 on. Before that the terms may grow (here they grow up to \frac{5^4}{4!} = \frac{5^5}{5!} \approx 26), but finitely many early terms don't matter (Changing a finite number of terms).

Convergence and boundedness

Theorem. Every real sequence with a finite limit is bounded.

Reason: For a convergent sequence, all sufficiently late terms satisfy \lvert a_n - a\rvert < 1. The finitely many earlier terms are bounded as well.

The converse is false: a_n = (-1)^n satisfies \lvert a_n\rvert \le 1 but has no limit. Boundedness alone does not imply convergence.

Why does the reason give an explicit bound?

With \varepsilon = 1 there is N with \lvert a_n - a\rvert < 1 for n \ge N, so \lvert a_n\rvert \le \lvert a_n - a\rvert + \lvert a\rvert < 1 + \lvert a\rvert there. The early terms a_1, \dots, a_{N-1} are finitely many numbers, and a finite set has a largest absolute value. So C = \max\{\lvert a_1\rvert, \dots, \lvert a_{N-1}\rvert, 1 + \lvert a\rvert\} satisfies \lvert a_n\rvert \le C for all n, which is "bounded" in the sense of 6 Sequences › Bounded and unbounded sequences. In practice the contrapositive is the useful form: unbounded ⇒ divergent (e.g. Fibonacci).

The monotone convergence theorem

Theorem (Weierstrass). A non-decreasing real sequence bounded above converges to its supremum. A non-increasing sequence bounded below converges to its infimum.

Examples: a_n = \frac{n}{n+1} \nearrow 1, b_n = \frac1n \searrow 0.

Two plots on the slide: \frac{n}{n+1} rising towards height 1, \frac1n falling towards 0.

Proof for a non-decreasing sequence. Assume a_{n+1} \ge a_n for every n and M = \sup\{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} < \infty. For any \varepsilon > 0, the number M - \varepsilon is not an upper bound. Hence some index N satisfies

M - \varepsilon < a_N \le M.

By monotonicity, for all n \ge N,

M - \varepsilon < a_N \le a_n \le M.

Therefore \lvert a_n - M\rvert < \varepsilon for all n \ge N, so a_n \to M. \square

Symbols
  • M — the supremum of the set of values, finite because the sequence is bounded above
  • \nearrow, \searrow — "increases to", "decreases to"
  • a_N — the term that beats M - \varepsilon, which exists by the \varepsilon-characterisation of the supremum (6 Sequences › Characterising the infimum and supremum)
Connection — this is where completeness is used

The proof needs M = \sup to exist as a real number, which is the completeness axiom (3 Set of Real Numbers › Completeness: no gaps). In \mathbb{Q} the theorem fails: 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \dots (decimal truncations of \sqrt2) is increasing, bounded and rational, but its limit \sqrt2 is not in \mathbb{Q}. The theorem is the first place where "\mathbb{R} has no gaps" turns into a practical tool: it proves convergence without knowing the limit in advance.

Worked example — monotone convergence for a_1 = 1, a_{n+1} = \sqrt{a_n + 6}
  1. Compute terms to guess: 1,\ 2.646,\ 2.940,\ 2.990,\ 2.998, \dots — rising, apparently towards 3.
  2. Bounded above by 3 (induction): a_1 = 1 < 3; if a_n < 3 then a_n + 6 < 9, so a_{n+1} < 3.
  3. Increasing: compare squares (all terms are positive): a_{n+1}^2 - a_n^2 = a_n + 6 - a_n^2 = (3 - a_n)(a_n + 2) > 0, since a_n < 3 by step 2. So a_{n+1} > a_n.
  4. Converges: increasing and bounded above, so a_n \to a for some a by the monotone convergence theorem, with 1 \le a \le 3.
  5. Find a by passing to the limit in the recursion: a_{n+1} \to a as well, and \sqrt{a_n + 6} \to \sqrt{a + 6}, so a = \sqrt{a + 6}, i.e. a^2 - a - 6 = (a - 3)(a + 2) = 0. Since a \ge 1, a = 3. Step 5 is only allowed after step 4: solving a = \sqrt{a + 6} finds the only possible limit, but doesn't prove that there is one.

Monotone but not bounded?

If (a_n) is non-decreasing and unbounded above, then a_n \to +\infty. Indeed, for every M > 0 some a_N > M; monotonicity gives a_n \ge a_N > M for n \ge N.

Contrast: a_n = n \to +\infty, while b_n = (-1)^n n is not monotone. Both are unbounded, but their long-term behaviour differs.

Corollary. Let (a_n) be a real sequence.

  • If (a_n) is non-decreasing, then it converges if and only if it is bounded above.
  • If (a_n) is non-increasing, then it converges if and only if it is bounded below.
Intuition

A monotone sequence has only two options: settle at a finite limit or run off to \pm\infty. It can never oscillate. So for monotone sequences the single question "is it bounded?" decides convergence.

Consider a_n = \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n. It is strictly increasing and bounded above, so it converges.

e = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n, \qquad e \approx 2.718281828\ldots
Symbols
  • e — Euler's number, the base of the natural exponential and logarithm (5 Functions › Exponential functions)
  • \frac1n — added to 1 before taking the n-th power

The monotonicity and bound can be proved using the binomial theorem.

Connection

In 6 Sequences › A sequence related to Euler's number the two bullet points "strictly increasing" and "bounded above" were stated without proof, with the remark that the values "get closer and closer to e". The monotone convergence theorem is what turns those two properties into an actual limit, and slide 38 supplies the proof of both.

Why the Euler sequence converges

Write a_n = (1 + 1/n)^n. The binomial theorem yields

a_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{k!} \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \left(1 - \frac{j}{n}\right).
Symbols
  • \sum_{k=0}^{n} — sum over the terms k = 0, 1, \dots, n of the binomial expansion
  • \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} — product over j = 0, \dots, k-1; for k = 0 the empty product is 1
  • k! — k factorial, 0! = 1
  • 1 - \frac{j}{n} — a factor between 0 and 1 that grows towards 1 as n grows

Increasing: For each fixed k, the product grows as n increases; a_{n+1} also has one additional positive term.

Bounded: Since every product is at most 1,

a_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{k!} < 3.

Thus (a_n) is increasing and bounded: a_n \to e.

Where does the formula come from, and why is \sum \frac{1}{k!} < 3?

Formula: the binomial theorem gives \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} \frac{1}{n^k}, and \binom{n}{k}\frac{1}{n^k} = \frac{1}{k!} \cdot \frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{n^k} = \frac{1}{k!} \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{n - j}{n}. (Checked exactly for n = 7 and n = 12.) Bound: for k \ge 1, k! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdots k \ge 2^{k-1} (each factor from 2 on is at least 2). So \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{1}{k!} \le 1 + \left(1 + \frac12 + \frac14 + \dots + \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right) < 1 + 2 = 3, using the geometric sum 1 + \frac12 + \frac14 + \dots < 2.

Two more representations of e

The same constant can be obtained in different ways:

e = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{1!} + \frac{1}{2!} + \dots + \frac{1}{n!}\right), \qquad e = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{\sqrt[n]{n!}}.
Symbols
  • 1 + \frac{1}{1!} + \dots + \frac{1}{n!} — the n-th partial sum of the factorial series (the leading 1 is the k = 0 term \frac{1}{0!})
  • \sqrt[n]{n!} — the n-th root of n factorial (which tends to +\infty, slide 31, but only about as fast as \frac{n}{e})

The factorial representation connects Euler's number to the exponential function and numerical approximation. Detailed proofs can be discussed separately.

Intuition

The two representations converge at very different speeds. The factorial sum is already correct to 15 digits after 18 terms, which is why it is used to compute e. The root formula is slow: at n = 2000 it gives only \approx 2.712. \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n is slow too (2.70481 at n = 100).

Subsequences

A subsequence of (a_n) is obtained by choosing indices n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots and taking

(a_{n_k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}.
Symbols
  • n_1 < n_2 < \dots — a strictly increasing choice of indices (natural numbers)
  • k — the new index: a_{n_k} is the k-th selected term
  • (a_{n_k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}} — the subsequence, itself a sequence

Example: from a_n = n choose the even indices: a_2, a_4, a_6, a_8, \dots = 2, 4, 6, 8, \dots Or choose squares: a_1, a_4, a_9, a_{16}, \dots = 1, 4, 9, 16, \dots

On the slide the selected terms are marked in orange on the number line.

Intuition

A subsequence is the original sequence with some terms deleted, infinitely many kept, and the order unchanged. You may skip, but not go back or repeat: a_2, a_1, a_3, \dots and a_1, a_1, a_2, \dots are not subsequences. Formally, k \mapsto n_k is a strictly increasing function \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}, and the subsequence is the composition k \mapsto a(n_k) (5 Functions).

Even and odd subsequences

The sequence a_n = (-1)^n has no limit, but its even- and odd-indexed terms each form a convergent subsequence.

  • Even indices: a_{2k} = 1 \implies a_{2k} \to 1.
  • Odd indices: a_{2k-1} = -1 \implies a_{2k-1} \to -1.

Selecting terms does not change their values or their order.

Properties of subsequences

Suppose (a_{n_k}) is a subsequence of (a_n).

  • If (a_n) is bounded above or below, then so is (a_{n_k}).
  • If a_n \to a \in \mathbb{R}, then a_{n_k} \to a.
  • If (a_n) is non-decreasing (or non-increasing), then so is its subsequence.

A divergent sequence may still have convergent subsequences. Conversely, two subsequences with different finite limits rule out convergence.

Why does every subsequence of a convergent sequence have the same limit?

Key fact: n_k \ge k for every k (induction: n_1 \ge 1, and n_{k+1} > n_k \ge k gives n_{k+1} \ge k + 1). Given \varepsilon, take N from a_n \to a. For k \ge N we have n_k \ge k \ge N, so \lvert a_{n_k} - a\rvert < \varepsilon. The same N works. The "conversely" sentence is the contrapositive: if a_n \to a, then every subsequence tends to a, so two subsequences with different limits are impossible. This is the quickest divergence proof in practice (see the worked example below).

Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem

Theorem. Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.

Example: a_n = (-1)^n is bounded but divergent; a_{2k} = 1 \to 1, a_{2k-1} = -1 \to -1.

Unbounded analogue: If a sequence is unbounded above, it has a subsequence tending to +\infty; similarly for unbounded below.

The finite subsequential limit is guaranteed only for bounded sequences.

Why is Bolzano–Weierstrass true? (sketch)
  1. Every sequence has a monotone subsequence. Call index m a "peak" if a_m \ge a_n for all n > m. If there are infinitely many peaks m_1 < m_2 < \dots, then a_{m_1} \ge a_{m_2} \ge \dots is non-increasing. If there are only finitely many, start after the last one: each index n there is not a peak, so some later term is larger, and repeating gives a strictly increasing subsequence.
  2. Bounded + monotone ⇒ convergent by the monotone convergence theorem.

So Bolzano–Weierstrass, too, rests on completeness. (The textbook alternative halves an interval containing infinitely many terms over and over.)

Subsequential limits and accumulation points

A real number a is a subsequential limit of (a_n) if some subsequence (a_{n_k}) converges to a.

Equivalent formulation: for every \varepsilon > 0 and N \in \mathbb{N}, some n \ge N satisfies \lvert a_n - a\rvert < \varepsilon.

Example:

a_n = (-1)^n + \frac1n, \qquad a_{2k} \to 1, \quad a_{2k-1} \to -1.
Symbols
  • a_{2k} = 1 + \frac{1}{2k} — the even-indexed terms; a_{2k-1} = -1 + \frac{1}{2k-1} — the odd-indexed terms

Thus -1 and 1 are its two finite accumulation points.

Connection

The equivalent formulation is word for word the definition of an accumulation point from 6 Sequences › Accumulation points of a sequence. So "accumulation point" and "subsequential limit" are the same thing, and the worked example (-1)^n + \frac1n there gets its second proof here. The chapter-6 board notes also list d_n = \sin\frac{\pi n}{2} (1, 0, -1, 0, \dots): its subsequences d_{4k-3} = 1, d_{2k} = 0, d_{4k-1} = -1 show the three accumulation points 1, 0, -1.

A unique subsequential limit is not enough

The sequence a_{2k-1} = 0, a_{2k} = 2k has only one finite subsequential limit, namely 0, but it is divergent:

0, 2, 0, 4, 0, 6, 0, 8, \dots

Odd indices converge to 0; even indices tend to +\infty.

A bounded sequence converges iff all its finite subsequential limits agree.

Consequences of Bolzano–Weierstrass

Let (a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} be a real sequence, and write \overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}.

  • Every sequence has at least one subsequential limit in \overline{\mathbb{R}}. If it is bounded, at least one such limit is finite.
  • A sequence converges in \mathbb{R} if and only if it is bounded and has exactly one subsequential limit.
  • A sequence is unbounded above (respectively, below) if and only if it has a subsequence tending to +\infty (respectively, -\infty).
  • A number a \in \overline{\mathbb{R}} is an accumulation point of (a_n) if and only if some subsequence (a_{n_k}) converges to a.
Worked example — divergence by two subsequences: a_n = (-1)^n \frac{n}{n+1}
  1. Split by parity: even n = 2k: a_{2k} = \frac{2k}{2k+1} \to 1; odd n = 2k - 1: a_{2k-1} = -\frac{2k-1}{2k} \to -1 (both by Another proof: n/(n+1) → 1).
  2. Conclude divergence: two subsequences with different limits, so (a_n) has no limit (Properties of subsequences).
  3. All subsequential limits: every subsequence has infinitely many even or infinitely many odd indices, so its limit (if any) is 1 or -1. Hence S = \{-1, 1\}, and \liminf a_n = -1, \limsup a_n = 1 (next section).
  4. Compare with inf and sup: terms -\frac12, \frac23, -\frac34, \frac45, \dots. All lie strictly between -1 and 1 and get arbitrarily close to both, so \inf a_n = -1 and \sup a_n = 1, not attained. Here inf/sup and liminf/limsup coincide; the next slides show they need not.

Limit inferior and limit superior

Let (a_n) be a real sequence. Denote by S the set of all its subsequential limits in \overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}. The limit inferior is the least subsequential limit, while the limit superior is the greatest:

\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n = \min S, \qquad \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n = \max S.
Symbols
  • S \subseteq \overline{\mathbb{R}} — the set of subsequential limits (= accumulation points, including \pm\infty); non-empty by Bolzano–Weierstrass

An equivalent definition using tails

For each N \in \mathbb{N}, consider only the terms with n \ge N. Their lower and upper bounds are

\ell_N = \inf_{n \ge N} a_n, \qquad u_N = \sup_{n \ge N} a_n \quad (\text{in } \overline{\mathbb{R}}).

Equivalent formulas:

\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n = \lim_{N \to \infty} \ell_N = \sup_{N \in \mathbb{N}} \inf_{n \ge N} a_n, \qquad \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n = \lim_{N \to \infty} u_N = \inf_{N \in \mathbb{N}} \sup_{n \ge N} a_n.
Symbols
  • the tail from N — the terms a_N, a_{N+1}, \dots
  • \ell_N — the infimum of the tail (its greatest lower bound); u_N — the supremum of the tail
  • \sup_{N} \inf_{n \ge N} a_n — the largest of the tail infima; \inf_N \sup_{n \ge N} a_n — the smallest of the tail suprema

Connection: For a_n = (-1)^n, every tail contains -1 and 1; thus \ell_N = -1 and u_N = 1 for all N. Both definitions therefore give \liminf a_n = -1 and \limsup a_n = 1.

Why does \lim_N \ell_N always exist, and why does it equal \sup_N \ell_N?

Going from the tail at N to the tail at N + 1 removes one term, and a smaller set has a larger (or equal) infimum: \ell_{N+1} \ge \ell_N. So (\ell_N) is non-decreasing, and by the monotone convergence theorem (with +\infty allowed when unbounded, Monotone but not bounded?) it tends to its supremum. Likewise (u_N) is non-increasing and tends to its infimum. This is why limsup and liminf exist for every sequence, while the limit need not.

Intuition — eventual floor and ceiling

u_N is the ceiling of everything that happens from time N on. As N grows, the early high terms drop out and the ceiling comes down; \limsup is where it ends up, the "eventual ceiling". \liminf is the "eventual floor". The sequence converges exactly when floor and ceiling meet.

Tail bounds: the example a_n = 1/n

For a_n = 1/n, the largest value remaining after index N is a_N = 1/N. The smallest possible tail bound is 0.

u_N = \sup_{n \ge N} \frac1n = \frac1N, \qquad \ell_N = \inf_{n \ge N} \frac1n = 0.
Symbols

As N increases, u_N moves down towards 0. The early value a_1 = 1 no longer determines the upper tail bound. (Plot on the slide: after N = 4, the highest remaining term is 1/4.)

\limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n = \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0.
Symbols
  • both equal 0 because u_N = \frac1N \to 0 and \ell_N = 0 for all N

For a bounded sequence these are the smallest and largest subsequential limits.

Tempting: "the lowest the sequence goes" = \liminf. But \inf can be decided by a single early term (a_1 = -2 above), while \liminf ignores any finite number of terms and only sees what happens in the long run. Always \inf a_n \le \liminf a_n \le \limsup a_n \le \sup a_n. They coincide only when the extreme values are approached in the tail, as in the worked example (-1)^n\frac{n}{n+1} above.

Cauchy sequences

Definition of a Cauchy sequence

A real sequence (a_n) is Cauchy if

\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists N \in \mathbb{N}\ \ \forall m, n \ge N : \quad \lvert a_m - a_n\rvert < \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • m, n — any two indices from N on (not necessarily neighbours, either may be larger)
  • \lvert a_m - a_n\rvert — the distance between two late terms
  • \varepsilon, N — tolerance and starting index, as in the definition of convergence

Interpretation: sufficiently late terms are close to one another. Unlike the definition of convergence, no candidate limit a appears.

Checking the Cauchy condition: a_n = 1/n

We want to make \lvert a_m - a_n\rvert small whenever both indices m and n are sufficiently large. Let \varepsilon > 0 and choose an integer N > 1/\varepsilon. Then for any m, n \ge N,

\left\lvert \frac1m - \frac1n \right\rvert \le \max\left\{\frac1m, \frac1n\right\} \le \frac1N < \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • \max\{\frac1m, \frac1n\} — the larger of the two terms; the distance between two numbers in (0, \frac1N] is at most the larger one

All late terms are between 0 and 1/N. So (1/n) is a Cauchy sequence.

Why neighbouring terms are not enough

It is not enough that consecutive differences \lvert a_{n+1} - a_n\rvert tend to zero.

Counterexample: harmonic partial sums

a_n = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n, \qquad a_{n+1} - a_n = \frac{1}{n+1} \longrightarrow 0,
Symbols
  • a_n — the n-th partial sum of the harmonic series \sum \frac1k; \frac{1}{n+1} — the term added in the next step

but (a_n) is not Cauchy: its terms grow without bound. The Cauchy condition compares all pairs of sufficiently late terms, not only neighbours.

Why is the harmonic sequence not Cauchy (and unbounded)?

Compare a_{2n} with a_n: a_{2n} - a_n = \frac{1}{n+1} + \dots + \frac{1}{2n}, which is n terms, each at least \frac{1}{2n}, so the gap is \ge n \cdot \frac{1}{2n} = \frac12. Both n and 2n are \ge N for n \ge N, so with \varepsilon = \frac12 the Cauchy condition fails for every N. Applying the same estimate repeatedly, a_{2^k} \ge 1 + \frac{k}{2}, which exceeds every bound. The steps shrink, but they shrink too slowly: their sum is still unbounded.

The Cauchy convergence criterion

Theorem. A real sequence converges to a finite real number if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.

Convergent ⇒ Cauchy: If a_n \to a, choose m, n so large that both errors are < \varepsilon/2. Then

\lvert a_m - a_n\rvert \le \lvert a_m - a\rvert + \lvert a_n - a\rvert < \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • \lvert a_m - a\rvert, \lvert a_n - a\rvert — the errors of two late terms; the triangle inequality goes "through" the limit a

Cauchy ⇒ convergent: A Cauchy sequence is bounded. By Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence; the Cauchy property forces the entire sequence to converge to the same limit. This direction uses completeness of \mathbb{R}.

Why is a Cauchy sequence bounded, and how does the subsequence "force" the limit?

Bounded: with \varepsilon = 1, all terms from N on satisfy \lvert a_n - a_N\rvert < 1, so they lie in (a_N - 1, a_N + 1); the finitely many earlier terms are bounded anyway (as in Convergence and boundedness). Forcing: let a_{n_k} \to a. Given \varepsilon, take N from the Cauchy condition with \frac\varepsilon2, and pick one k with n_k \ge N and \lvert a_{n_k} - a\rvert < \frac\varepsilon2. Then for every n \ge N: \lvert a_n - a\rvert \le \lvert a_n - a_{n_k}\rvert + \lvert a_{n_k} - a\rvert < \varepsilon. The late terms are all close to one term, which is close to a.

Intuition — why bother with Cauchy?

To use the definition of convergence you must already know the limit a. Often you don't: an iterative solver produces x_1, x_2, \dots precisely because the answer is unknown. The Cauchy criterion lets you prove convergence from the terms alone, and it is the mathematical basis of the usual stopping rule "stop when successive iterates barely change" — with the warning of the harmonic example that "successive" must really mean "all late pairs".

A recursive Cauchy sequence

Let a_1 = 1 and a_{n+1} = 1 + \frac{1}{a_n}:

1,\ 2,\ \frac32,\ \frac53,\ \frac85,\ \dots

Why does it converge? For n \ge 2, a_n \in \left[\frac32, 2\right], and

\lvert a_{n+1} - a_n\rvert = \frac{\lvert a_n - a_{n-1}\rvert}{a_n a_{n-1}} \le \frac23 \lvert a_n - a_{n-1}\rvert.
Symbols
  • a_n — the n-th term; numerators and denominators are consecutive Fibonacci numbers (6 Sequences › The Fibonacci sequence)
  • \left[\frac32, 2\right] — the closed interval containing every term from a_2 on
  • \frac23 — a contraction factor: each step is at most \frac23 of the previous one

Differences shrink geometrically, giving a Cauchy sequence.

If a_n \to a, then

a = 1 + \frac1a \implies a^2 - a - 1 = 0.

Since a > 0,

a = \frac{1 + \sqrt5}{2}.
Symbols
  • a — the limit; \frac{1 + \sqrt5}{2} \approx 1.618 — the golden ratio (the other root \frac{1 - \sqrt5}{2} is negative)
Why the difference formula, the bound, and why geometric shrinking gives Cauchy?

Formula: a_{n+1} - a_n = \frac{1}{a_n} - \frac{1}{a_{n-1}} = \frac{a_{n-1} - a_n}{a_n a_{n-1}}; take absolute values. Bound: a_n a_{n-1} = \left(1 + \frac{1}{a_{n-1}}\right) a_{n-1} = a_{n-1} + 1 \ge 2, so the factor \frac{1}{a_n a_{n-1}} is at most \frac12 \le \frac23; the slide's \frac23 is a safe, slightly generous constant. (And a_n \in [\frac32, 2] by induction: if a_n \in [\frac32, 2] then \frac{1}{a_n} \in [\frac12, \frac23], so a_{n+1} \in [\frac32, \frac53].) Cauchy: with q = \frac23 and d = \lvert a_3 - a_2\rvert, \lvert a_{k+1} - a_k\rvert \le d\,q^{k-2}. For m > n \ge 2, the triangle inequality over the steps gives \lvert a_m - a_n\rvert \le d\,(q^{n-2} + q^{n-1} + \dots) = \frac{d\,q^{n-2}}{1 - q}, which tends to 0 (Powers). Newton's iteration for √2

Recall a_1 = 1 and a_{n+1} = \frac12\left(a_n + \frac{2}{a_n}\right). A useful identity:

a_{n+1} - \sqrt2 = \frac{\left(a_n - \sqrt2\right)^2}{2a_n}.
Symbols
  • a_n - \sqrt2 — the error of the n-th approximation; the identity says the next error is the square of the current one, divided by 2a_n
  • a_n > 0 for all n (induction: averages of positive numbers are positive)

For n \ge 2 we have a_n \ge \sqrt2 and a_{n+1} \le a_n, so the sequence converges by the monotone convergence theorem.

Passing to the limit in the recurrence gives

a = \frac12\left(a + \frac2a\right) \implies a^2 = 2,

so the positive limit is \sqrt2.

Symbols
  • a — the limit of (a_n); positive, because a_n \ge \sqrt2 for n \ge 2 and limits preserve \ge (Passing inequalities to the limit)
Why a_n \ge \sqrt2 and a_{n+1} \le a_n from n = 2 on?

Identity: \frac12\left(a_n + \frac{2}{a_n}\right) - \sqrt2 = \frac{a_n^2 - 2\sqrt2\,a_n + 2}{2a_n} = \frac{(a_n - \sqrt2)^2}{2a_n}. Above \sqrt2: the right side is a square over a positive number, so a_{n+1} \ge \sqrt2 for every n \ge 1, i.e. a_n \ge \sqrt2 for n \ge 2. (a_1 = 1 is below; that's why the slide starts at n = 2.) Decreasing: a_{n+1} - a_n = \frac{2 - a_n^2}{2a_n} \le 0 when a_n \ge \sqrt2. So from a_2 on the sequence is non-increasing and bounded below by \sqrt2: it converges, and the recurrence pins the limit down. This answers slide 2's question ("Do the terms really approach \sqrt2?") with a proof.

Intuition — why it converges so fast

"The new error is the old error squared (over about 2\sqrt2)" means the number of correct digits roughly doubles per step: errors \approx 0.09, 0.0025, 0.000002 for a_2, a_3, a_4. This quadratic convergence is why Newton-type methods are used in robotics and numerical solvers. The robot of slide 3, whose error only halves per step, gains about one binary digit per step — the difference between 4 steps and 50 steps for 15 digits.

Key Facts

  • Finite convergence: a_n \to a means \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists N : \lvert a_n - a\rvert < \varepsilon for every n \ge N.
  • Monotonicity and bounds: Bounded non-decreasing / non-increasing sequences converge. Their limits are \sup a_n / \inf a_n.
  • Subsequences: Every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit. Bounded sequences have convergent subsequences.
  • Cauchy criterion: (a_n) converges in \mathbb{R} iff all sufficiently late terms are uniformly close to one another.
